primary_topics: Keynote address at the Second National Congress of the Clergy (NCC II), World Trade Center, January 28, 2010 -- invited by Ambassador Tita de Villa; speaking to 5,000+ ordained priests about the testimony of a public servant's personal relationship with the Lord

The National Bilibid Prison visit: CJP's most unforgettable experience as a jurist -- Matthew 25 compelled him to visit despite security warnings; 500 inmates; 30 whom he had personally sentenced raised their hands; none felt wrongly sentenced; he spoke boldly of hope

The inmate's challenge: a life termer asked why CJP consigned him to prison when the priest merely counseled him, asked him to pray the rosary, and forgave him -- 'in the name of love, why can't you just follow my confessor's example?'

CJP's theological resolution: God is both the Lord of justice and the Lord of love; the judge-daughter parable (paid the fine himself because she was his daughter) as the governing image of the Father who sent His Son to redeem mankind
sub_topics: CJP speaking before 5,000 priests: 'I am used to listening to priests delivering their homilies, not to talking before them'; invited by Amb. Tita de Villa as National Coordinating Committee chairperson

Special Minister of Holy Communion: became one in 1989 (21 years ago); continued after SC appointment (1995); when named CJ, Fr. Antonio Rosales asked if he would still want to continue and what special arrangements/protocol he needed; CJP: 'in Santuario de San Antonio, I was just an ordinary parishioner'

Matthew 25 and the prison visit: security warned against going to the National Bilibid Prison; the Gospel reading was Matthew 25 (Final Judgment: visiting the imprisoned); 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to risk the ire of the Lord!'

The prison scene: several hectares, fruit trees and shrubs; makeshift auditorium on the greeneries; 500 inmates; 'when I arrived they thundered into applause'; asked how many he had personally sentenced to life imprisonment or death -- about 30 sheepishly raised their hands; asked how many felt wrongly sentenced -- 'to my great relief, no one raised his or her hand'

Speaking boldly of hope: 'almost everyone in the world is in some kind of prison -- many rich people are imprisoned by their greed; others by incurable illnesses; some by their minds'; those behind bars have hope because one day they would serve their sentences and be freed

The inmate's question: a life termer introduced himself and asked the justice-vs-love contrast: 'after confessing my sins, the priest merely counseled me, then asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me. In the name of love, why can't you just follow my confessor's example?'

CJP's reflection: led him back to Matthew 25 -- 'the Lord too was making choices because He was the Lord of justice just as He is likewise the Lord of love'; 'just as there are human and physical laws, there are spiritual laws'; both criminal and sinner must repent, restitute and reform; 'both the judge and the priest must guide the criminal and the sinner towards these three Rs of salvation in civil and spiritual life'

The judge-daughter parable: a policeman brings a young lady to a judge for speeding along Ayala Avenue; the judge rules a P500 fine; then descends, removes his robe, goes to the cashier and pays the P500 himself -- 'because the young, repentant lady who promised to reform her life and who did not have money to pay the fine was his daughter'; 'He had to let justice be done. But because he loved his daughter, he sacrificed his own money. And so it is with our Father in heaven.'

stances.claim: The inmate's question -- 'In the name of love, why can't you just follow my confessor's example?' -- is the deepest theological challenge CJP faced in his judicial career. His answer: God is BOTH the Lord of justice and the Lord of love; the judge-daughter parable shows that these are not in opposition but that love sometimes requires paying justice's price on behalf of the beloved. The three Rs of salvation (repent, restitute, reform) apply equally to the criminal in civil law and the sinner before God.
stances.rhetorical_move: justice-and-love-as-inseparable-pair: the inmate's question as the catalyst for the most profound theological synthesis in the corpus
stances.confidence: asserted as a theological reflection informed by personal judicial experience

stances.claim: CJP's refusal to accept any special protocol as CJ at his parish ('I was just an ordinary parishioner') before 5,000 priests is the governing example of equality before God. The message is aimed directly at the clerical audience: they should apply the same principle of spiritual equality in their service.
stances.rhetorical_move: ordinary-parishioner-testimony: CJP's personal practice of equality before God as the governing illustration for a clerical audience about the same principle

notable_anecdotes: Matthew 25 compels the prison visit: 'I decided to accept the invitation after attending Holy Mass in which the Gospel reading was Matthew 25... about our Lord asking whether His disciples visited Him when He was in prison. So, I told myself, better to risk the ire of the inmates than to risk the ire of the Lord!'

30 raised hands, zero wrongly sentenced: '500 inmates... I began by asking how many of them I have personally sentenced to life imprisonment or to death. About 30 of them sheepishly raised their hands. Then I courageously asked how many of them felt they had been wrongly sentenced. To my great relief, no one raised his or her hand.'

The life termer's justice-vs-love question: 'all the commandments of the Lord can be summed up in one sentence, love God and love your fellow beings? Why then did you have to consign me to prison? Contrast this with the way our Church treats sinners. After confessing my sins, the priest merely counseled me, then asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me.'

The judge-daughter parable: the judge fines his daughter P500 for speeding; descends from the rostrum, removes his robe, goes to the cashier, and pays the fine himself. 'He had to let justice be done. But because he loved his daughter, he sacrificed his own money... And so it is with our Father in heaven.'

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 28, 2010 as the keynote at the Second National Congress of the Clergy (NCC II) at the World Trade Center -- invited by Ambassador Tita de Villa; speaking to 5,000+ priests ('I am used to listening to priests delivering their homilies, not to talking before them') -- this address by CJP opens with his testimony as Special Minister of Holy Communion since 1989 at Santuario de San Antonio, continuing even after becoming CJ ('in Santuario de San Antonio, I was just an ordinary parishioner; no special arrangements or protocols'). His most unforgettable judicial experience was visiting the National Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa -- security warned against it, but the Mass Gospel (Matthew 25: 'I was in prison and you visited me') compelled him: 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to risk the ire of the Lord!' At a makeshift auditorium with 500 inmates, he asked how many he had personally sentenced to life or death -- about 30 sheepishly raised their hands -- then asked how many felt wrongly sentenced: 'to my great relief, no one raised his or her hand.' He spoke of hope: everyone is in some kind of prison (greed, illness, mental incapacity); those behind bars will one day be freed. Leaving, a life termer posed the deepest theological question CJP faced: 'all the commandments can be summed up as love God and love your neighbor -- why then did you consign me to prison? After confessing my sins, the priest merely asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me. In the name of love, why can't you follow my confessor's example?' CJP's reflection (back to Matthew 25): God is BOTH the Lord of justice and the Lord of love; both criminal and sinner must repent, restitute and reform; both judge and priest guide them toward these three Rs of salvation. He closes with the judge-daughter parable: a judge fines his speeding daughter P500, then descends from the rostrum, removes his robe, goes to the cashier and pays the fine himself -- 'He had to let justice be done. But because he loved his daughter, he sacrificed his own money. And so it is with our Father in heaven.'
